about: An example shape already split into equal parts appears, and the child taps another shape split into the same number of equal parts — even when the pieces are shaped differently, like a square cut corner-to-corner and a square cut straight down the middle that both show two equal halves. It's a free, interactive Grade 2 geometry activity that plays right in the browser with no sign-up.

The big idea is that equal shares of the same whole do not have to look alike. The other choices show the shape split into unequal parts, split into the wrong number of parts, or not split at all, so the child has to focus on the count of equal pieces rather than on the picture matching exactly. The child recognizes the matching partition; the child does not cut the shapes.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.G.A.3 — recognizing that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape, and naming shares as halves, thirds, and fourths. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.

Use the words halves, thirds, and fourths for equal shares
howToPlay: Look at the example shape and see how many equal parts it is split into.
Tap the other shape split into the same number of equal parts, even if the pieces look different, then press Check.
Try again any time; there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Recognize shapes split into two, three, or four equal shares — the focus of Common Core 2.G.A.3
Understand that equal shares can have different shapes as long as the parts are the same size
Strengthen the fair-share thinking that names and compares fractions later

about: Four pictures of the same shape appear — a circle, a square, or a rectangle — and the child taps the one divided into equal halves or equal fourths, learning to spot when a shape has been cut into fair shares before ever writing a fraction. Everything turns on one word: equal. In each round the other three pictures are the same shape cut into unequal parts, split into the wrong number of parts, or marked with a line that does not really divide it — so a child cannot win just by picking 'a shape with a line in it.' They have to look closely and decide whether the pieces are truly the same size, which is what makes halves and fourths meaningful.
It is aligned to Common Core 1.G.A.3 — recognizing shapes divided into two and four equal shares and describing them as halves and fourths. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.

howToPlay: Read or listen to the prompt — find the shape split into equal halves, or equal fourths.
Look at the four shapes and tap the one whose pieces are truly the same size, then press Check.

learningGoals: Recognize circles, squares, and rectangles divided into two or four equal shares — the focus of Common Core 1.G.A.3

about: Longer words break into beats the ear can catch: looking at a picture, the child taps the syllables in the right order to build it — rab-bit, muf-fin, car-rot, ti-ger — working through familiar words like balloon, pencil, and penguin. Understand that longer words are built from smaller syllable beats.

about: Two everyday objects sit side by side and the child taps the taller, the longer, or the shorter one — comparing real, familiar pictures like a pine or palm tree, a pencil, crayon, marker or ruler, a carrot or cucumber, a giraffe, a sunflower, or a candle. learningGoals: Directly compare two objects and describe which is taller, longer, or shorter — the focus of Common Core K.MD.A.2.

about: "Make 3," "Make 7," "Make 10" — the child builds the number by tapping squares on a single ten-frame to drop in exactly that many animal counters, then presses Check. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten counting activity for numbers 0 to 10 that runs in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

The ten-frame is what makes this more than rote counting. Its two rows of five give each number a shape a child can recognize — four fills most of the top row, ten fills the whole frame — so counting starts to connect to how much a number really is. The child decides how many animals to place and can add or take some away before checking, which keeps the focus on one-to-one counting rather than guessing.
It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.B.4 — understanding the relationship between numbers and quantities and connecting counting to cardinality. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.

Placing one counter per square with careful one-to-one counting
Seeing each number 0 to 10 take shape on the two-row ten-frame
Connecting the spoken or written number to a real quantity
howToPlay: Read the prompt to see which number to make, like Make 7.
Tap the squares of the ten-frame to place exactly that many animal counters, then press Check.
Not quite? Add or remove counters and try again — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Make any number from 0 to 10 with counters on a ten-frame — the focus of Common Core K.CC.B.4
Connect counting to how many, so the last number counted tells the quantity
Build the ten-frame number sense that early addition and place value depend on

about: The prompt names a number to make, and the child taps the squares of a double ten-frame to fill in exactly that many pieces of fruit across the two frames, then presses Check. Working all the way to 20 means a full ten plus some more. This free, interactive Kindergarten counting activity plays in the browser with no sign-up.

The double ten-frame teaches the most important idea about teen and twenty numbers: a full ten plus some more. To make 14, the child fills the first frame to ten and then adds four onto the second — so the structure of the number, ten and four, is right there to see. Working past ten is a genuine step beyond counting to ten, and the two frames give the child a way to keep the count organized instead of losing track.
It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.B.4 — connecting counting to cardinality and extending number sense beyond ten. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.

howToPlay: Read the prompt to see which number to make, up to 20.
Tap the squares of the double ten-frame to place exactly that many fruit counters, then press Check.
Not quite? Add or remove counters and try again — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Make any number from 0 to 20 with counters on a double ten-frame — the focus of Common Core K.CC.B.4
See numbers past ten as a full ten and some extra ones
Build the counting-on and place-value foundation for first-grade math

about: A ten-frame shows a group of animal counters and asks one simple question: how many? The child counts the animals — anywhere from 0 to 10 — and types the matching numeral on the keypad. This is the answering side of counting. Instead of building a number, the child reads a quantity that is already there and names it with a written number. Because the counters sit in the two rows of a ten-frame, a child can begin to recognize amounts at a glance — a full top row is five, a full frame is ten — and check by counting one by one. That move from counting to a single written numeral is the heart of cardinality.
It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.B.5 — counting to answer "how many?" questions about objects arranged on a frame. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.

Matching a counted quantity to its numeral 0 to 10

learningGoals: Count to answer how many about up to ten objects — the focus of Common Core K.CC.B.5
Name a quantity with the matching written numeral
Build the cardinality that reading and writing numbers depends on

about: A double ten-frame shows a group of fruit counters, and the child writes the numeral for how many — counting anywhere from 0 to 20 and typing the number on the keypad. Because a full frame is ten, the child can count on for the teen and twenty numbers. This free, interactive Kindergarten counting activity runs in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

The child reads a quantity that is already laid out across two ten-frames and names it with a written numeral, including the harder two-digit numbers past ten. Because a full frame is ten, the child can count on from ten for the teen and twenty numbers rather than starting at one every time, and then record what they counted as a written number — the connection between amount and symbol.

Counting on from a full ten for teen and twenty numbers
Connecting a quantity to its written number symbol

Type that number on the keypad, including numbers past ten, and press Check.

learningGoals: Represent a count of up to 20 objects with a written numeral — the focus of Common Core K.CC.A.3
Write the numbers 0 to 20, including two-digit numbers
Build the read-and-write number skill that all later math notation depends on

about: The prompt names a teen number like 16, and the child fills the first ten-frame to a complete ten and then adds the extra ones onto a second frame — so 16 shows up as ten and six more. Building it this way makes the hidden structure visible. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten place-value activity that plays in the browser with no sign-up.

Teen numbers are tricky because their names hide their structure — "sixteen" does not say "ten and six." Building each one on two frames makes that hidden structure visible: there is always one full ten and then some ones. The child is composing the number from a ten and extras rather than counting all the way up by ones, which is the very idea that place value is built on.
It is aligned to Common Core K.NBT.A.1 — composing and decomposing numbers from 11 to 19 into a ten and some ones. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.

Building each teen number 11 to 19 as a ten and some more

howToPlay: Read the prompt to see which teen number to make.
Fill the first ten-frame to ten, then place the extra ones on the second frame, and press Check.
Not quite? Adjust the counters and try again — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Compose teen numbers 11 to 19 as a ten and some ones — the focus of Common Core K.NBT.A.1
Understand that every teen number contains one complete ten
Build the place-value foundation for adding and grouping in first grade

about: Children work out cards like 2 + 3 and 9 − 4 (both 5), or 3 + 4 and 9 − 2 (both 7), then tap an addition and the subtraction with the same answer to link the pair. It's a free, interactive Grade 1 math activity that runs right in the browser, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is that an addition expression and a subtraction expression can be worth the same amount — the equal sign means "the same as," not "here comes the answer." The cards do not show their totals, so children must actually compute each one and then hunt for a different-looking expression with the matching value. Every round has two (sometimes three) values to find, mixing plus and minus facts together.

It is aligned to Common Core 1.OA.D.7 — understanding the meaning of the equal sign and deciding whether equations involving addition and subtraction are true. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.

Match a plus fact to a minus fact that has the same answer
Understand the equal sign as meaning "the same amount as"
Compare two different-looking expressions for equal value
howToPlay: Work out each card — additions like 4 + 5 and subtractions like 10 − 1.
Tap an addition, then tap the subtraction with the same answer, and watch the pair link.
Find both equal pairs in the round — there is no timer and no score, so take your time.
learningGoals: Understand that addition and subtraction expressions can be equal — the focus of Common Core 1.OA.D.7
Read the equal sign as "the same as" rather than "the answer is next"
Build flexible fact fluency by linking plus and minus facts that share a value

about: A mixed pile of friendly pictures appears — some animals like a cat, dog, duck, or fish, and some fruit like an apple, banana, orange, or strawberry, all jumbled together — and when the prompt names one group, such as animals, the child decides how many pictures belong to it and taps the matching number. It's a free Kindergarten activity that plays in the browser with no account needed.

The pictures are mixed on purpose. To answer how many animals there are, a child cannot simply count everything on the screen — they have to look at each picture, decide what it is, set aside the fruit that does not belong, and count only the group that was asked for. That quiet two-step of sorting first and counting second is the whole heart of the activity, and it is a genuinely different skill from counting a row of identical objects.
It is aligned to Common Core K.MD.B.3 — classifying objects into given categories and counting how many are in each. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Looking at a mixed set of animals and fruit and deciding which group each picture belongs to
Counting only the pictures in the named group and ignoring the rest
Telling the count of one group apart from the total number of pictures
Building the sort-first, count-second habit that early data and graphing work rely on

Decide how many pictures belong to that group, then tap the number that matches.
A warm check confirms a correct count and offers an easy retry whenever you need it.
learningGoals: Classify pictures into given categories and count how many are in each — the focus of Common Core K.MD.B.3.

about: One everyday object appears and the child taps the word that best describes it — long, tall, or heavy. The objects are chosen so one attribute clearly stands out: a pencil and a carrot are long, a giraffe is tall, and a rock and a pumpkin are heavy. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten measurement activity that plays right in the browser, with no account needed.

The whole point is to put words to the ways we measure things before any numbers or rulers appear. A child does not count or measure here; they look at a real object and decide which measurable attribute fits — length, height, or weight. Because each pictured object has one obviously strongest attribute, the child practices noticing what kind of measurement a thing invites, which is the language foundation under all later measuring.
It is aligned to Common Core K.MD.A.1 — describing measurable attributes of an object such as length, height, and weight. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Match an object to the measurement word that fits it — long, tall, or heavy
Tell length, height, and weight apart as different ways to measure
Look at a real object and decide what kind of measurement it invites

learningGoals: Describe an object's measurable attributes — length, height, weight — the focus of Common Core K.MD.A.1

about: Marigold the mole runs a Knowing Machine that builds new words by snapping a prefix or suffix onto a root: kind, lucky, tell, color, fear, or help drops in, a cog stamped un-, re-, -ful, or -less clicks on, and the child reads what it makes — unkind, retell, colorful, fearless — then taps what it now means. It's a free, browser-based Grade 2 reading activity that needs no account or download.

The work is meaning, not memorizing. For unkind the choices are 'kind,' 'not kind,' and 'full of kindness,' so the child has to know that un- flips a word to its opposite, while -ful means 'full of' and -less means 'without.' Later rounds turn it around: the machine shows a meaning like 'to tie it again' or 'without any use,' and the child taps the affix (re-, less) that builds it, proving the part-to-meaning link both directions.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.4.b and L.2.4.c — using a known prefix or suffix as a clue to the meaning of a new word. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Knowing that un- means not, re- means again, -ful means full of, and -less means without
Reading a built word like unhappy or spotless and choosing the meaning that fits
Working backward from a meaning to the prefix or suffix that makes it
Telling apart -ful and -less, which attach to the same root but mean opposite things
howToPlay: Drop the un-, re-, -ful, or -less cog onto the root word in Marigold's Knowing Machine and read the new word it builds.
Tap the choice that tells what the new word means; in the 'which one' rounds, read the meaning first and tap the affix that builds it.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Use common prefixes and suffixes as clues to a word's meaning — the focus of Common Core L.2.4.b.
Understand that un- reverses a word while -ful and -less point in opposite directions.
Build the word-part habit that helps a child unlock new vocabulary while reading independently.

about: Children build a rectangular array — equal rows lined up in columns — then find how many dots there are in all, in this free, interactive Grade 2 math activity that plays right in the browser with nothing to install and no sign-up. The rounds grow from a small 2-by-3 array up through 3-by-4, 2-by-5, 4-by-4, and 4-by-3, so the child fills tidy grids of different shapes.

The big idea is that a rectangle of equal rows can be added the fast way. As the child taps to fill each row, a repeated-addition strip builds underneath — 4 + 4 + 4 — so they see four counted three times rather than counting every dot one at a time. Then they type the total on the keypad. Seeing the rows line up as equal addends is exactly the bridge from addition into multiplication.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.OA.C.4 — using addition to find the total number of objects arranged in a rectangular array of rows and columns, and writing an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Filling a rectangular grid as equal rows and columns
Reading the array as repeated addition, such as 4 + 4 + 4 = 12
Counting by equal groups instead of by ones to find a total
Typing the total that matches the rows the child just built
howToPlay: Look at the array Bot needs — for example, 3 rows of 4 — and tap to fill in each row.
Watch the repeated-addition strip add the equal rows up, then type how many there are in all on the keypad.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Find the total in a rectangular array using repeated addition — the focus of Common Core 2.OA.C.4.
See equal rows as equal addends and write the matching sum.
Build the equal-groups foundation that multiplication grows out of in later grades.

about: Children make equal groups — the same number of objects in each — and add them up to find the total, in this free Grade 2 math activity that plays in any browser with no download and no account. The rounds run from 2 groups of 3 up to 3 groups of 5, including 4 groups of 4 and 5 groups of 2, so the child works with many different equal-group arrangements.

Unlike a tidy rectangular array, here the objects sit in separate groups, which makes the 'same number in each' idea the whole point. As the child fills each group, a repeated-addition strip grows alongside — 4 + 4 + 4 — turning the equal groups into a sum, and then they type how many in all. The child builds and adds the groups; they do not multiply yet, but they meet the exact thinking multiplication is built on.
It is aligned to Common Core 2.OA.C.4 — using repeated addition of equal addends to find a total. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Making several groups that each hold the same number
Adding equal groups as repeated addition, such as 4 + 4 + 4 = 12
Telling equal groups apart from groups of different sizes
Finding a total by counting groups rather than counting by ones
howToPlay: Read how many equal groups to make and how many go in each one, then tap to fill the groups.
Watch the equal groups add up on the repeated-addition strip, then type the total on the keypad.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Find a total from equal groups using repeated addition — the focus of Common Core 2.OA.C.4.
Understand that the groups must be equal for the same-addend sum to work.
Build the equal-groups sense that multiplication depends on in later grades.

about: Atlas the armadillo keeps a file of true facts, and the child reads one of his short cards — two real sentences such as 'Bees live in a hive. They make sweet honey.' — then answers a question about it. The facts cover bees, frogs, the sun, penguins, spiders, trees, cows, and rain, so children practice on friendly nonfiction. It's a free Kindergarten reading activity that runs in the browser with no account.

Each round asks a who, what, where, or how-many question — 'Where do bees live?' or 'How many legs does a spider have?' — and offers three answers. Two are wrong on purpose ('in a nest,' 'in a pond'), so a child cannot pick by feel; they have to look back at the sentence and find the words that actually answer the question. That look-back-and-find move is the heart of reading nonfiction for details.
It is aligned to Common Core RI.K.1 — asking and answering questions about key details in an informational text. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Reading a short two-sentence fact about a real thing
Finding the words that answer a who, what, where, or how-many question
Looking back at the text instead of guessing the answer
Telling the right detail apart from two believable wrong choices
howToPlay: Read Atlas's two-sentence fact card — for example, the one about bees and their hive.
Read the question and tap the answer you found in the fact, from the three choices.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Answer questions about key details in a fact text — the focus of Common Core RI.K.1.
Locate who, what, where, and how-many details right in the sentences.
Build the habit of reading nonfiction closely and checking the text for answers.

about: At The Harbor Post, Marlow the pelican hands the child short notes to sort by why their author wrote them: a note about owls hunting at night is there to inform, one about Pip the puppy chasing his tail is there to entertain, and one that begins 'To make a paper boat, first fold the paper in half' is there to instruct. It's a free Grade 2 reading activity that plays in the browser with no sign-up.

The three bins — 'To tell facts,' 'To tell a fun story,' and 'To show how to do it' — make the author's job visible. The child reads each note and decides its purpose from how it is written: real-world facts, a silly little tale, or step-by-step directions with words like first, next, and then. They are judging the writer's intent, not just the topic, which is what makes author's purpose a thinking skill rather than a guess.
It is aligned to Common Core RI.2.6 — identifying the main purpose of a text, including what the author wants to answer, explain, or describe. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Deciding whether a note is meant to inform, entertain, or instruct
Spotting real facts versus a made-up, playful story
Recognizing how-to directions by their step words like first, next, and then
Judging why a writer wrote something, not just what it is about
howToPlay: Read the short harbor note Marlow hands you.
Send it to the right bin — to tell facts, to tell a fun story, or to show how to do it.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Identify whether a text is written to inform, entertain, or instruct — the focus of Common Core RI.2.6.
Use clues in the writing, such as facts or step-by-step directions, to find the author's purpose.
Build the reader's awareness of why authors write, which supports comprehension across texts.

about: Bea the bookworm keeps two bookshelves — one for make-believe story books and one for fact books about real things — and the child helps her shelve them right. Three covers appear, each with a title and a one-line blurb, such as 'The Sleepy Dragons' (two dragons look for a nap), 'All About Real Bugs' (where bugs live), and 'Diggers and Cranes' (how real machines lift and dig). It's a free Grade 1 reading activity that runs in any browser with no account.

Bea asks for either a story book or a fact book, and the child taps the cover that fits. The blurbs are the clue: dragons looking for a nap and a goblin hunting socks are pretend, while bones in your body and how bees make honey are real. Because every round mixes a true book in with the pretend ones, the child has to read each blurb and decide make-believe or real — the first step in telling literature from informational text.
It is aligned to Common Core RL.1.5 — explaining major differences between books that tell stories and books that give information. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Reading a book's title and blurb to decide what kind of book it is
Telling a make-believe story from a book of real facts
Choosing the story book, or the fact book, that Bea asks for
Noticing clues like dragons and goblins versus bones, bees, and machines
howToPlay: Read the three book covers on Bea's shelf, with their titles and blurbs.
Tap the book Bea asks for — a make-believe story, or a book of real facts.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Tell story books apart from fact (informational) books — the focus of Common Core RL.1.5.
Use a short blurb to decide whether a book is make-believe or real.
Build early awareness of genre that supports both reading for fun and reading to learn.

about: Bingo the beagle sniffs out the exact right word: a picture appears — a cat, hat, cup, dog, pig, bed, net, or pan — alongside three little words that look almost the same but differ by one letter, like cat, cot, and cut, and the child sounds out each and taps the one that names the picture. It's a free Kindergarten decoding activity that plays right in the browser with no download and no account.

The three choices change only the middle vowel (cat / cot / cut) or another single letter (pin / pan / pen), so a child cannot win by glancing at the first letter. To find the match they must read all the way through and hear the vowel sound — a is not o is not u. Attending to the letters that actually differ is precisely the decoding move this round trains.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.K.3.d — distinguishing between similarly spelled words by identifying the sounds of the letters that differ. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Sounding out short CVC words letter by letter
Hearing the middle vowel that makes cat, cot, and cut different
Reading the whole word instead of guessing from the first letter
Matching the word that truly names the picture
howToPlay: Look at Bingo's picture and read the three look-alike words underneath.
Sound each one out and tap the word that names the picture.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Tell similarly spelled words apart by the letters that differ — the focus of Common Core RF.K.3.d.
Decode short CVC words by reading every sound, including the vowel.
Build the careful, all-the-way-through reading that accurate decoding depends on.

about: Booker the bear keeps the glossary and shows the child what the two words at the top of a dictionary page are for: two guide words sit at the top — like cap and cot — and the child taps the one word, from choices such as car, can, and cup, that would actually appear on that page because it falls between them in ABC order. It's a free Grade 2 vocabulary activity that runs in the browser with no account.

Guide words are a real reference tool, and the only way to use them is to compare letters in order. Between cap and cot, the word car fits (it comes after cap and before cot), while can comes too early and cup comes too late. Because the choices share their first letters, the child has to look at the second and third letters to decide — the exact alphabetizing skill that makes a dictionary or glossary usable.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.4.e — using glossaries and beginning dictionaries to find the meaning of words. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Reading the two guide words at the top of a glossary page
Putting words in alphabetical order by their second and third letters
Deciding which word falls between the guide words
Ruling out words that come too early or too late in ABC order
howToPlay: Look at Booker's two guide words at the top of the page.
Tap the word from the three choices that belongs on this page — the one that comes between them in ABC order.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Use guide words to find a word in a glossary or dictionary — the focus of Common Core L.2.4.e.
Alphabetize words by looking past the first letter to the next ones.
Build the reference-skill confidence that helps a child look up word meanings on their own.

about: Bo the bunny is stocking his winter pantry, where a sealed crate holds exactly ten berries — so a crate just is a ten. The child reads a pile of berries, a written numeral like 63, or a question such as 'how many is forty?', then slings the berries to the shelf showing the right number of crates (tens) and loose berries (ones). It's a free Grade 1 place-value activity that plays in the browser with no sign-up.

Every shelf is a trap or a match, which is what builds real place-value sense. For 34 the choices include the true 3 tens and 4 ones, the digit-flipped 4 tens 3 ones, a near-miss with the wrong tens, and a value trap. Trickier rounds offer a regrouping trap (1 ten and 15 loose ones for 25) or ask the child to name a hoard of 8 tens and 5 ones as 85 — not 58 and not 805. The child must read the tens and ones, not just match digits.
It is aligned to Common Core 1.NBT.B.2 — understanding that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Reading a two-digit number as a count of tens and ones
Knowing that a sealed crate of ten berries stands for one ten
Catching digit-flip traps like 34 versus 43
Spotting that 1 ten and 15 loose ones is not yet tidied into the right tens and ones
howToPlay: Read Bo's pile, numeral, or question to find the number he needs.
Sling the berries to the shelf with the right crates (tens) and loose berries (ones), and watch the crates count by tens.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Understand a two-digit number as tens and ones — the focus of Common Core 1.NBT.B.2.
Tell true place value apart from digit-flip and grouping traps.
Build the bundling-by-ten sense that all later two-digit arithmetic rests on.

about: Bram the beaver runs a board shop where every order is a length story the child models on a measuring tape — gluing two boards together, sawing a piece off a 50 cm plank, or measuring how much longer a 60 cm shelf is than a 45 cm desk. The stories add and subtract lengths within 100 centimeters. It's a free Grade 2 measurement activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

What makes it more than arithmetic is that the unknown moves around. Sometimes the result is missing, sometimes a part, sometimes the change, the start, or the difference. The child reads the order, places each known length into the right spot on a bar, change, or compare diagram — leaving out the decoy tile that doesn't belong — marks the mystery length, and dials the answer in centimeters. Mapping the words onto the diagram is the modeling skill this round builds.
It is aligned to Common Core 2.MD.B.5 — using addition and subtraction within 100 to solve word problems involving lengths in the same units. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Reading a length word problem and picturing it on a measuring tape
Placing the known lengths into the right spots on a part, change, or compare diagram
Finding the unknown whether it is the result, a part, the change, the start, or the difference
Ignoring the decoy length that does not belong in the problem
howToPlay: Read Bram's order and decide what each length is — a whole, a part, a start, a change, or a difference.
Place each known length on Bram's diagram, mark the mystery length, and dial the answer in centimeters.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Solve length word problems by adding and subtracting within 100 — the focus of Common Core 2.MD.B.5.
Model a problem with a diagram and find the unknown in any position.
Build the problem-modeling habit that supports measurement and multi-step word problems.

about: At Bramble's berry-juice stand, two containers appear — like a tall skinny glass beside a short wide bowl — and the child predicts which holds more juice, then pours to find out. It's a free Kindergarten activity built around one question, which cup holds more, and it plays in the browser with no download and no account.

The whole point is that your eyes can fool you: a tall, narrow glass can look like it holds the most yet hold less than a low, wide dish. The child compares the two containers directly, makes a call, and watches the juice pour to check it, building the idea that 'holds more' is about capacity, not height. Some rounds ask which is the same, or whether one container's juice fits inside the other — no counting and no numbers anywhere.
It is aligned to Common Core K.MD.A.2 — directly comparing two objects with a measurable attribute in common and describing which holds more or less. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Comparing two containers to tell which holds more or less juice
Looking past how tall or wide a container looks to its real capacity
Predicting first, then pouring to check the prediction
Recognizing when two different-looking cups hold the same amount
howToPlay: Look at the two containers and call which one holds more berry juice before Bramble pours.
Watch the juice pour to see if your prediction was right.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Directly compare two containers and tell which holds more, less, or the same — the focus of Common Core K.MD.A.2.
Understand that capacity is not the same as how tall a container looks.
Build the compare-by-an-attribute thinking that measurement and data grow from.

about: Bundle Bot is a little robot who loves tidying loose ones into neat tens, and he needs the child's help: to build a number like 23, 34, or 45, the child drops in loose ones, and the moment there are exactly ten, they pull the lever to clunk those ten ones into one neat ten. Numbers run up to forty-nine. It's a free Grade 1 place-value activity that plays in the browser with no account.

The lever only works on exactly ten, which is what teaches the rule that ten ones make one ten. Some rounds turn it around — unbundling 32 into 2 tens and 12 ones — and others set a trap, like an impostor pile of nine ones that is not ready to bundle, or an overfill the child must catch. Across all of them the child is physically grouping by ten, the concrete meaning behind the tens digit of every two-digit number.
It is aligned to Common Core 1.NBT.B.2.a — understanding that a bundle of ten ones is called a ten. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Counting loose ones and knowing when there are exactly ten
Bundling ten ones into one ten, and unbundling a ten back into ten ones
Building two-digit numbers up to forty-nine from tens and ones
Catching an impostor pile of nine that is not ready to bundle
howToPlay: Read Bundle Bot's target number and add loose ones into the machine.
When there are exactly ten loose ones, pull the lever to bundle them into one neat ten, and keep going until the number is built.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Understand that ten ones make one ten — the focus of Common Core 1.NBT.B.2.a.
Bundle and unbundle tens to build and take apart two-digit numbers.
Build the grouping-by-ten foundation that place value and regrouping depend on.

about: A single letter appears — like D, F, or M — and the child taps the picture whose name begins with that letter's sound, choosing from familiar groups such as animals, food, and everyday objects (a dog, a fish, a moose, a tiger). It's a free Kindergarten phonics activity that runs right in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

Each round shows one correct picture and three that start with other sounds, so the child cannot guess — they have to say each picture's name and listen for the very first sound. Connecting the letter D to the /d/ at the start of 'dog' is the core letter-sound link, and hearing it against fish, rabbit, and tiger makes that first sound stand out clearly.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.K.3.a — knowing the primary sound that each consonant letter represents. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Connecting a letter to the sound it makes
Saying a picture's name and listening for its first sound
Matching the beginning sound to the letter shown
Telling the right first sound apart from three other beginnings
howToPlay: Look at the letter at the top, like D, and say its sound.
Tap the picture whose name begins with that sound, from the four choices.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Know the primary sound each consonant letter makes — the focus of Common Core RF.K.3.a.
Hear and match the first sound in a spoken word to its letter.
Build the letter-sound foundation that sounding out and reading words depend on.

about: Two two-digit numbers appear — like 47 and 52, or 63 and 38 — and the child taps the statement that is true, using greater than (>), less than (<), and equal to (=). Some pairs are equal, such as 45 and 45 or 88 and 88, so the equal sign matters too. It's a free Grade 1 place-value activity that runs right in the browser with no sign-up.

The strategy is to look at the tens first, then the ones. With 47 and 52, the 5 tens beat the 4 tens, so 47 is less than 52 — even though 7 is bigger than 2. Tricky pairs like 29 and 92 use the same digits in different places, so the child must read place value rather than the digits themselves. Choosing the correct symbol turns that comparison into the formal language of >, =, and <.

It is aligned to Common Core 1.NBT.B.3 — comparing two two-digit numbers based on the meanings of the tens and ones digits, recording the result with the symbols >, =, and <. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Comparing two two-digit numbers by their tens, then their ones
Choosing the right symbol — greater than, less than, or equal to
Recognizing when two numbers are equal
Reading place value in tricky pairs like 29 and 92
howToPlay: Look at the two two-digit numbers, checking the tens digit first and then the ones.
Tap the statement that is true, using >, =, or <.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Compare two-digit numbers and record the result with >, =, and < — the focus of Common Core 1.NBT.B.3.
Use the meaning of the tens and ones digits to decide which number is greater.
Build the place-value comparison skill that larger-number work later depends on.

about: A single shape appears and the child counts its straight sides, then taps the number that matches — a triangle with 3 sides, a square with 4, a pentagon with 5, or a hexagon with 6, with number choices drawn from a pool of 3 through 8. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten geometry activity that runs right in the browser on a tablet, phone, or classroom computer, with nothing to install and no sign-up.

The big idea is that a shape is more than its name — it is made of parts you can count. A child cannot win by recognizing 'a triangle'; they have to trace each edge with their eyes and count the sides one at a time. Because the number tiles include near-misses like 5 next to 6, miscounting by one shows up, which nudges careful, finger-on-each-side counting rather than a quick guess.
It is aligned to Common Core K.G.B.4 — analyzing and comparing shapes by describing their parts, such as the number of sides. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Count the straight sides of a triangle, square, pentagon, and hexagon
Connect a shape to a number — how many sides it has, not just its name
Count carefully one side at a time instead of guessing the total at a glance
Tell shapes apart by their parts, like five sides versus six
howToPlay: Look at the shape on the board and count its straight sides, one by one.
Tap the number that matches how many sides you counted, then press Check.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Count the number of sides on common shapes — the focus of Common Core K.G.B.4
Describe a shape by its parts rather than only naming it
Build the careful-counting and shape-analysis habits that later geometry depends on

about: A number from 1 to 20 appears and the child decides whether it is even or odd, then taps the Even or Odd tile. With just the two choices, the child judges every number on its own — is it the kind that pairs up evenly, or the kind with one left over? It's a free, interactive Grade 2 number activity that runs in the browser with no sign-up.

The big idea is that even and odd are about whether a count can be split into two equal groups with nothing left over. A child is not adding or subtracting here; they are sorting whole numbers by structure. Working across the whole range from 1 to 20, with both choices always present, builds the quick recognition — and the habit of checking the ones place — that makes even and odd feel automatic.
It is aligned to Common Core 2.OA.C.3 — determining whether a group of objects has an odd or even number of members. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Decide whether a number from 1 to 20 is even or odd
Understand even numbers as pairs with nothing left over, and odd as one extra
Look at the ones digit as a quick way to tell even from odd
Sort whole numbers by their structure rather than by adding or subtracting
howToPlay: Look at the number shown on the board.
Decide if it is even or odd and tap the matching tile, then press Check.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Tell whether a number up to 20 is even or odd — the focus of Common Core 2.OA.C.3
Explain even as pairs with none left over and odd as one extra
Build the number sense that supports later work with equal groups and multiplication

about: One shape appears at a time and the child taps whether it is flat or solid — flat (2D) shapes like a circle, triangle, square, and hexagon, and solid (3D) shapes like a cube, sphere, cylinder, and cone. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten geometry activity that plays right in the browser on tablets, phones, and computers, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is the difference between a shape you could draw on paper and a shape you could pick up and hold. A child is not naming the shapes here; they are sorting them into two-dimensional and three-dimensional. Mixing familiar flat shapes with their solid cousins — a circle next to a sphere, a square next to a cube — makes the child look at whether a shape has depth, which is the first step toward understanding solids.
It is aligned to Common Core K.G.A.3 — identifying shapes as two-dimensional (flat) or three-dimensional (solid). No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Tell flat (2D) shapes apart from solid (3D) shapes
Recognize a circle, square, and triangle as flat, and a cube, sphere, and cone as solid
Notice whether a shape has depth — something you could hold versus draw
Sort shapes into two groups instead of only naming them
howToPlay: Look at the shape on the board.
Decide whether it is flat or solid and tap the matching tile, then press Check.
Try again any time; there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Identify shapes as flat (two-dimensional) or solid (three-dimensional) — the focus of Common Core K.G.A.3
Connect a flat shape to its solid relative, like a square and a cube
Build the foundation for naming and describing 3D shapes later

about: A group of friendly pictures appears — like one owl, four foxes, or eight elephants — and the child counts the objects and taps the matching numeral. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten counting activity that runs right in the browser on a tablet, phone, or classroom computer, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is cardinality — that the last number you say when counting tells how many there are in all. Because the objects appear in lines, little arrays, and scattered bunches, the child cannot rely on a memorized pattern; they have to count each picture once and only once. The number choices sit close together, like 7, 8, and 9, so an off-by-one count shows up and invites a careful recount.
It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.B.5 — counting to answer 'how many?' for up to 10 objects in a line, an array, or a scattered arrangement. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Count up to 10 objects and say how many there are in all
Count each picture exactly once, whether it sits in a row or scattered
Match a counted amount to its written numeral
Build cardinality — knowing the last number counted is the total
howToPlay: Look at the group of pictures and count them carefully, one at a time.
Tap the number that matches how many you counted, then press Check.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Count up to 10 objects in any arrangement and name the total — the focus of Common Core K.CC.B.5
Connect a count to its written numeral
Build the one-to-one counting and cardinality that all later math rests on

about: One letter appears and the child taps the matching letter in its other form — uppercase to lowercase, or lowercase to uppercase. A big B is shown and the child finds the small b; a big R finds r; a big E finds e. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten reading activity that plays right in the browser with no sign-up.

The big idea is that every letter has two looks that name the same letter. The wrong choices are deliberately close — for B the small letters offered are b, d, p, and h — so a child has to know the real shape of the letter, not just pick something rounded. Sorting out the letters that flip and turn, like b and d, is exactly the careful looking that builds confident letter recognition.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.K.1.d — recognizing and naming all upper- and lowercase letters of the alphabet. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Match an uppercase letter to its lowercase form, and the other way around
Recognize the same letter in both its big and small shapes
Tell apart look-alike letters like b, d, and p
Build the secure letter recognition that fluent reading needs
howToPlay: Look at the letter shown on the board.
Tap its matching letter in the other case — big or small — then press Check.
Try again any time; there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Recognize and name upper- and lowercase letters — the focus of Common Core RF.K.1.d
Connect each letter's two forms as one letter
Steady the look-alike letters that young readers often mix up

about: A number from 1 to 9 appears and the child taps the number that comes right after it — see a 4 and find the 5, see an 8 and find the 9. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten counting activity that runs right in the browser on tablets, phones, and computers, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is counting forward from a number you are given, instead of always starting over at one. The choices come from numbers 0 through 10 sitting near the right answer, so the child has to truly know what comes next rather than guessing. That skill — picking up the count in the middle of the sequence — is what lets counting become quick and flexible.
It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.A.2 — counting forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Name the number that comes right after a given number from 1 to 9
Count forward starting in the middle of the sequence, not from one
Know the order of numbers well enough to spot the next one
Build flexible counting that does not need a fresh start each time
howToPlay: Look at the number shown on the board.
Tap the number that comes right after it, then press Check.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Count forward from a given number — the focus of Common Core K.CC.A.2
Know which number comes next in the sequence to 10
Build the counting fluency that addition and number sense build on

about: The child hears the ending chunk of a word and sees its first letter, blends the two together into a word, then taps the picture it names — for c + 'at', the child blends to 'cat' and finds the cat. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten reading activity that plays right in the browser with no sign-up.

The big idea is blending — pulling a first sound and a word-ending together to make a whole word. One of the picture choices rhymes with the answer (a bat sits next to the cat), so the rime alone is not enough; the first letter is the clue that decides which word it is. The child listens, blends, and reads the picture rather than matching letters on the page.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.K.2.c — blending and segmenting the onsets and rimes of single-syllable spoken words. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Blend a first sound and a word-ending into a whole word
Use the first letter as the clue when two pictures rhyme
Hear that words like cat and bat share an ending but start differently
Connect a blended spoken word to the picture it names
howToPlay: See the first letter and listen to the word's ending sound.
Blend them together in your head, then tap the picture they make and press Check.
Try again any time; there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Blend onsets and rimes into single-syllable words — the focus of Common Core RF.K.2.c
Tell rhyming words apart by their beginning sound
Build the blending skill that turns letters into reading

about: Two written numbers appear and the child taps the bigger one — like 7 and 6, or 8 and 7. Some pairs are far apart, such as 9 and 2, and some are right next to each other, such as 8 and 7. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten counting activity that runs in the browser on tablets, phones, and computers, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is comparing numbers as numerals, not as groups of objects to count. There are no pictures to lean on — the child has to know that 8 is more than 7 just by reading the figures. The close pairs are what make this real practice: a child cannot win by spotting a 'bigger-looking' number; they have to know the value each numeral stands for.

Read a measuring scale starting from zero

about: The child hears a common high-frequency word spoken aloud, then taps the matching written word among look-alike choices — everyday sight words like was, the, of, you, see, and, go, and like that appear constantly in early texts. about: A prompt names a shape — circle, square, triangle, rectangle, hexagon, oval, star, diamond, heart, or pentagon — and the child finds it by sight, tapping it from four pictured choices. about: A number like 34, 57, 60, or 82 pops up with the words ten more or ten less, and the child works it out in their head and taps the answer from four choices. about: Two groups of friendly pictures appear side by side — cats, dogs, ducks, fish, apples, bananas, oranges, or strawberries — and the child taps the group that has more. about: A load of crates, passengers, or coal rolls into the switchyard on numbers like 4, 5, 6, 7, and 10, and the track forks into two cars. The heart of the activity is that one number can be broken apart in more than one way. about: An everyday event is paired with a time — you eat breakfast at 7:00, the sun comes up at 6:00, you eat dinner at 6:00, you look at the stars at 9:00 — and the child decides whether it happens in the a.m. (morning) or p.m. (afternoon or evening). The child reads the hands, counts on the minutes, and taps the matching digital time from three cards, in this free Grade 3 time activity that plays right in the browser with no sign-up.

Every round here counts forward, and most of them cross the next hour, which is the part that trips children up. Three o'clock plus thirty is an easy 3:30, but 3:45 plus 30 must roll past four to 4:15, 10:50 plus 20 jumps to 11:10, and 2:15 plus 45 lands exactly on 3:00. The two wrong cards are deliberately tempting — a time that forgot to roll the hour, or one that added the minutes the lazy way — so the only sure path is to count on carefully and carry the hour.

Connect a counted-on time to its written digital form

Carry the hour confidently when minutes cross the top of the clock.
Build the elapsed-time sense children use to figure out 'how long until' in everyday life.

about: Owl's Cuckoo Cottage makes the child the timekeeper for Owl's whole cozy day: read the wall clock and tap what Owl is doing — breakfast at 7:00, garden time at 3:00, lunch at 12:00, supper at 6:30, bedtime at 8:30 — and set the clock by dragging the hands so the cuckoo can pop out. What makes the game work is that it never lets a child win by the hour hand alone. Reading rounds, setting rounds, sky-cue rounds, and a 'which clock matches' ordering round keep the same idea fresh from several angles.

Match a clock time to the event that happens then in Owl's day
Connect the time of day to a real-world cue like dawn or midday

Link clock times to the familiar moments of a daily routine.

about: A written time is given — like 3:00, 7:30, 9:00, 6:30, or half past one — and the child drags the long and short hands on the analog face to show it while a digital readout updates as they go. practices: Drag the hour and minute hands to show a given time

Tell hours from half-hours and set each correctly

Check your clock and adjust as often as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Set an analog clock to the hour and half-hour — the focus of Common Core 1.MD.B.3.
Understand that at half past, the hour hand sits between two numbers.
Connect the analog clock face to the digital time children read every day.

about: A written time appears — 3:15, 7:45, 6:10, 9:20, 4:40, 1:50, 10:05, or 12:25 — and the child drags the analog clock's hands to show it, with a digital readout updating as they move. Reading and setting to five minutes means the minute hand finally matters in detail: quarter past puts it on the 3, quarter to puts it on the 9, ten past on the 2, and the child counts by fives around the face to land it exactly. The trickier times — like 7:45, where quarter to eight is written 7:45 rather than 8:45 — push children to read the hour hand as it creeps toward the next number. practices: Set the minute hand to a five-minute mark by counting by fives

Fine-tune the hands as often as you like — there is no timer and no score.

Count by fives around the clock to place the minute hand exactly.
Read times like quarter to eight correctly as 7:45 rather than 8:45.

about: Clunk the snack-robot needs an exact number of crunch-units — 8, 10, 12, or 14 — but his adding chip is cracked, so the child fills his lunchbox by tapping number-snacks off a wall (tiles like 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8) until they add up, then feeds him to check. The twist is the whole point: after one way works, the child makes the same total a brand-new way, in this free Kindergarten math game that plays in the browser with no sign-up.

Decomposing a number is a different skill from adding to a single answer, and the game is built so a child meets it from many sides. Some rounds are wide open — make 10 any way you like — while others add a rule: Clunk already holds 6, so add just enough to reach 10; use exactly three snacks; only certain tiles are allowed; or the box is too full, so take some away. Because there is no single right pile, children discover that 6 and 4, 7 and 3, and 8 and 2 are all ten, which is exactly the flexible number sense the activity is after.

learningGoals: Break a number up to ten into two or more parts — the focus of Common Core K.OA.A.3.
See that a number like 10 can be made several different ways.
Build the flexible part-whole sense that addition and subtraction grow from.

about: Pip the otter runs a seaside stall, and each round is a short word problem with real U.S. coins — penny, nickel, dime, and quarter: count a pile (two dimes and three pennies make 23¢), pay an exact price, make change when cheese costs 70¢ and you pay a dollar, or trade a quarter for smaller coins of equal value. The catch that makes it real money sense: the value is not printed on the coin, so a child has to know that a dime is worth 10¢ even though it is smaller than the 5¢ nickel. That breaks the natural habit of judging worth by size, and the variety of jobs — counting, paying exactly, making change, trading equal values — means children practice the meaning of each coin instead of one memorized routine. about: Comet the kangaroo lands on a three-digit number — 247, 362, 415, 683 — and makes a leap of 10 more, 10 less, 100 more, or 100 less; the child works it out mentally and types where Comet lands on the keypad. Comet's Big Leaps is a free Grade 2 math activity about adding and subtracting 10 and 100 in your head that plays right in the browser with no sign-up.

The activity is designed to build place-value intuition rather than counting. Because the child types the answer instead of choosing from cards, there is no guessing — they have to find the one digit that moves and leave the rest alone, which is the heart of mental ten- and hundred-jumps.

about: Children steer Captain Quill's raft downriver, and at each bend two number-buoys appear — like 7 and 6, or 5 and 6 — with a prompt to choose the bigger or the smaller one. The numbers are deliberately close together, so a child cannot just grab the obviously-larger one — telling 7 from 6 means actually reading the numerals. about: Skip the squirrel welds two word-blocks together — fish and bowl, milk and jug, egg and cup, foot and ball — and the child works out what the new word means from its parts; a fishbowl is a bowl for fish, not a bowl made of fish. about: Nib the apostrophe-spirit shows two words — do and not, it and is, you and are, I and am — and the child picks the contraction that drops the right letters and puts the apostrophe in exactly the right spot, making don't, it's, you're, and I'm. about: A picture appears — ship, chin, frog, flag, drum, crab, sled, clock — and the child taps the sound chunks in order to build the word, choosing the right opening pair from look-alike chunks, with a Hear it button to check by sound. The activity makes the difference between a blend and a digraph concrete. Building the word chunk by chunk, then hearing it, ties the spelling to the sounds rather than to memorized shapes.

about: A picture appears — cat, dog, pig, sun, bus, hat, fox, bun, and more — and the child taps the correct letters to build the consonant-vowel-consonant word that names it, choosing from the right letters mixed with a few distractors. about: A picture appears — kite, cake, rose, cube, cone, gate, nose, vase — with the base word already started, and the child taps the magic e to finish it, choosing it from a few other ending letters, then hears the long-vowel word read aloud. about: Daisy the duck plates up orders that always ask for several — 'I'd like two ___,' 'Wash all six ___,' 'I packed two ___' — so the child reads the request and taps the word that names more than one, choosing forms like cups, dishes, and boxes. The game teaches that English does not always add a plain s. Build the grammar foundation that early speaking and writing rely on.
