Later rounds ask the child to choose the right feature for a job — the glossary tells a word's meaning, the contents shows the topic, the index gives the page — so they learn what each text feature is actually for.

It is aligned to Common Core 1.RI.5 — knowing and using text features such as headings, tables of contents, glossaries, and icons to locate key facts. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Reading a table of contents, heading, glossary, index, and labeled diagram to find a fact
Matching a question to the spot in the text that answers it, instead of guessing
Knowing what each text feature does — meaning, topic, or page number
Using captions and labels on a diagram to learn what a part does
howToPlay: Read the question, like 'Which part helps it glow?'
Read the text feature on the page — the contents, glossary, diagram, or index.
Tap the part that holds the answer; try again as needed, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Use text features to locate key facts in an informational text — the focus of Common Core 1.RI.5
Choose the right feature for the job — glossary for meaning, contents for topic, index for page
Build the nonfiction navigation skills that make research reading possible

about: Fixit the repair-mole needs the missing number to fix each broken gadget, so the child finds the unknown part of an equation — the missing sum (8 + 5 = ?), a missing addend (8 + ? = 13), a missing subtrahend (13 − ? = 8), or a missing minuend (? − 5 = 8) — then drops it in and watches the gadget whir to life. It's a free, interactive Grade 1 math game played in the browser on any device with no sign-up.

The big idea is that the equals sign means 'the same as,' so the unknown can sit in any position, not just at the end. Early rounds let the child count countable objects and even count on or count back; later rounds fade the supports and use fact-family triangles, recombining, and a balance round like 6 + 6 = ? + 4 where both sides must match. The child reasons about the whole and its parts instead of just adding from left to right.
It is aligned to Common Core 1.OA.D.8 — determining the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation with the unknown in any position. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Finding the unknown in any spot — the sum, an addend, the subtrahend, or the minuend
Counting on and counting back to find a missing part
Using fact families to relate addition and subtraction
Balancing both sides of an equation so they are truly equal
howToPlay: Read the broken gadget's equation and see which number is missing.
Work out the missing part — count on, count back, or use the fact family.
Pop your answer in to fix the gadget; try again freely, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Find the unknown number in an addition or subtraction equation in any position — the focus of Common Core 1.OA.D.8
Understand the equals sign as 'the same amount on both sides'
Build the part-whole and fact-family reasoning that fluent computation depends on

about: Pip the fox takes a chocolate order like three fourths, then the child picks the unit piece by its size — there are no labels to read — and forges it the right number of times along the bar. Rounds cover halves, thirds, fourths, sixths, and eighths, including 3/4, 2/3, 3/8, and 5/6. It's a free, interactive Grade 3 fractions activity that runs in the browser on any device, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is that a fraction is built from copies of a unit fraction: 3/4 is three of the one-fourth pieces. Because the molds are shown by size, not labeled, the child has to judge which piece fits the whole bar the right number of times — one round even offers an unequal mold to reject, and another asks the same 3/4 on a bigger bar to show the share looks larger when the whole is larger. There are also 'name the unit' rounds where the bar is already split and the child picks the fraction for one part.
It is aligned to Common Core 3.NF.A.1 — understanding a fraction 1/b as one part of a whole split into b equal parts, and a/b as a parts of size 1/b. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Choosing a unit-fraction piece by its size, with no labels to lean on
Building a fraction as repeated copies of the unit piece — 3/4 as three fourths
Telling equal partitions from unequal ones, and rejecting the unfair mold
Seeing that the same fraction of a bigger whole is a bigger amount
howToPlay: Read Pip's order, like 'Forge three fourths.'
Pick the piece whose size fits the bar the right number of times.
Forge it that many times to fill the order; try again freely, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Understand a/b as a copies of the unit fraction 1/b — the focus of Common Core 3.NF.A.1
Connect the denominator to the size of the equal part and the numerator to how many
Build the part-by-part meaning of fractions that comparing and equivalence rely on

about: Crumb the mouse shows a piece cut one way, then three more cut into more or fewer slices, and the child taps the one that is the same amount — the equivalent fraction — for pairs like 1/2 and 3/6, or 3/4 and 6/8. Each fraction appears as a shaded bar beside its numbers, so the size is visible. It's a free, interactive Grade 3 fractions activity that plays in the browser on any device, with no sign-up.

The big idea is that different fractions can name the very same amount. The reference fraction (such as 1/2, 1/3, 2/3, or 3/4) sits beside three candidates that are cut into different numbers of slices, and only one shades the same length of bar. The other choices are close but wrong — for 1/2 the decoys might be 2/6 or 5/6 — so the child compares the shaded amounts, not just the numbers, and learns to look past 'different numbers' to 'same size.'
It is aligned to Common Core 3.NF.A.3 — recognizing and generating simple equivalent fractions and explaining why they are equal. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Recognizing that two fractions with different numbers can be the same amount
Comparing shaded bars to judge which fraction matches the reference
Connecting the picture of a fraction to its numerator and denominator
Spotting close-but-wrong fractions that shade more or less of the bar
howToPlay: Look at Crumb's reference piece and how much of the bar it shades.
Compare the three candidates — each cut into a different number of slices.
Tap the one that shades the same amount; try again freely, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Recognize simple equivalent fractions like 1/2 = 3/6 — the focus of Common Core 3.NF.A.3
Understand that equivalence is about equal amounts, not matching numbers
Build the equivalence sense needed for comparing and adding fractions later

about: Children tap the dotted lines to split a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares — 2 rows and 3 columns, 3 rows and 4 columns, on up to 4 rows and 5 columns — then type how many squares there are in all. It's a free, interactive Grade 2 geometry activity that runs in the browser on any device, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is that a rectangle can be split into equal squares laid out in neat rows and columns, and the rows-and-columns structure helps you count them. Because the child makes the grid themselves and then counts, they begin to feel that 3 rows of 4 squares means counting by equal groups — the quiet beginning of arrays and multiplication. The squares are all the same size on purpose, so 'how many' is a true total of equal parts.
It is aligned to Common Core 2.G.A.2 — partitioning a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and counting to find the total number. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Splitting a rectangle into equal rows and columns of same-size squares
Building a grid by tapping the dividing lines
Counting the squares to find the total in the rectangle
Noticing the rows-and-columns structure that leads toward arrays
howToPlay: Tap the dotted lines to make rows and columns of equal squares.
Build the grid the round asks for, like 3 rows and 4 columns.
Type how many squares there are in all — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Partition a rectangle into same-size squares and count the total — the focus of Common Core 2.G.A.2
See a rectangle as rows and columns of equal parts
Build the array foundation that prepares children for multiplication

about: A shape appears — a circle, square, rectangle, triangle, ellipse, diamond, hexagon, or pentagon — and the child taps the cutting lines to split it into 2 equal parts (halves) or 4 equal parts (fourths). It's a free, interactive Grade 1 geometry activity that plays in the browser on any device, with no sign-up.

The big idea is that equal shares must be fair — the pieces have to be the same size. Cutting a variety of shapes, not just circles, shows that halves and fourths are about equal area, not one familiar picture: a square cut into a grid of four and a circle cut into four both make fourths. Because the child does the cutting, they make the parts equal themselves rather than recognizing a finished picture.
It is aligned to Common Core 1.G.A.3 — partitioning circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares and describing them as halves and fourths. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Cutting circles, squares, and other shapes into equal parts
Making 2 equal shares (halves) and 4 equal shares (fourths)
Keeping the pieces the same size so the shares are fair
Seeing halves and fourths across many different shapes
howToPlay: Look at the shape and the number of equal parts to make.
Tap the cutting lines to split it into halves or fourths.
Make sure the pieces are equal — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Partition shapes into two and four equal shares — the focus of Common Core 1.G.A.3
Describe the equal parts as halves and fourths
Build the fair-share foundation that later fraction work depends on

about: A circle, triangle, hexagon, square, rectangle, diamond, or ellipse appears, and the child taps the cutting lines to divide it into three equal pieces — thirds. It's a free, interactive Grade 2 geometry activity that runs in the browser on any device, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is that thirds are trickier than halves because three equal pieces do not fall on an obvious middle line. A circle is split with three lines from the center, a rectangle into three equal strips, a triangle into three matching parts — so the child learns that 'thirds' means three same-size shares however the shape is cut. Making the cuts themselves builds the feel for equal partitioning that just looking at a picture cannot.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.G.A.3 — partitioning circles and rectangles into two, three, or four equal shares and describing the shares using the word thirds. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Cutting a shape into 3 equal parts
Making thirds across circles, rectangles, triangles, and more
Keeping all three pieces the same size
Using the word thirds for three equal shares
howToPlay: Look at the shape you need to cut into 3 equal parts.
Tap the cutting lines to make thirds.
Check that the three pieces are equal — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Partition shapes into three equal shares and name them thirds — the focus of Common Core 2.G.A.3
Understand that thirds must be three same-size parts, however the shape is cut
Strengthen the equal-partitioning sense that fractions build on

about: Big and Bit cross a bridge by comparing their groups of friends: the child pairs the two groups one-to-one, counts, and decides which has more, which has fewer, or whether they are the same. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten activity that plays in the browser on any device, with no sign-up.

The big idea is that you cannot tell which group is bigger just by how much space it takes up. The activity deliberately uses eye-tricks — a spread-out row of 5 placed beside a tight bunch of 6, or a scattered 7 beside a clustered 8 — and even a round where both groups have 5 but look different, so the child learns that rearranging things does not change how many there are. Pairing friends one-to-one and counting is what settles it. Some rounds also ask the child to make the groups equal or build a matching group.

It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.C.6 — identifying whether the number of objects in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number in another group. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Pairing two groups one-to-one to compare them
Deciding which group has more, fewer, or the same
Ignoring how spread out or bunched the objects look
Making two groups equal by adding to the smaller one
howToPlay: Look at Big and Bit's two groups of friends.
Pair them one-to-one and count to see which has more or fewer.
Tap your answer — or build a matching group when asked — with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Compare two groups as greater than, less than, or equal — the focus of Common Core K.CC.C.6
Understand that spreading objects out does not change how many there are
Build the one-to-one comparing skill that grounds early number sense

about: Gabby the goose explores funny sayings that don't mean what the words say — the child reads an idiom in a sentence, like 'It's raining cats and dogs,' 'a piece of cake,' 'hold your horses,' or 'let the cat out of the bag,' and taps what it really means. It's a free, interactive Grade 3 vocabulary game that runs in the browser, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is that figurative language carries a meaning beyond the literal words. In every round one wrong choice is the funny literal picture (cats and dogs truly falling, an actual potato on the couch), which is exactly the trap, and another choice is simply off. So the child cannot pick the words at face value — they have to think about what the saying means when people really use it.
It is aligned to Common Core L.3.5.a — distinguishing the literal and nonliteral meanings of words and phrases in context. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Reading a common idiom inside a real sentence
Choosing what a saying really means, not what the words literally say
Spotting and setting aside the funny literal picture
Understanding everyday figurative language people actually use
howToPlay: Read the saying in Gabby's sentence, like 'hold your horses.'
Think about what it really means, beyond the literal words.
Tap the real meaning — try again freely, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Tell the literal and nonliteral meanings of phrases apart — the focus of Common Core L.3.5.a
Interpret common idioms from how they are used in a sentence
Build the figurative-language understanding that deepens reading comprehension

about: Gauge the goat estimates how big real things are just by picturing them — the child reads a question, like about how long is an ant, a crayon, or a train, or how tall is a door, a school bus, or a flagpole, and taps the estimate that makes sense in centimeters or meters. It's a free, interactive Grade 2 math game that plays in the browser, with no sign-up.

The big idea is that good estimating means knowing the size of familiar things and choosing a sensible unit. Each round offers three numbers, and the wrong ones are believable distractors: an ant could be 1, 12, or 30 centimeters, and only 1 cm is reasonable; a door is 1, 2, or 9 meters, and 2 m fits. The child has to picture the real object and decide which number and unit actually match, rather than measuring anything.
It is aligned to Common Core 2.MD.A.3 — estimating lengths using units of centimeters and meters. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Picturing the real size of a familiar object
Choosing a sensible length estimate from believable choices
Knowing when to think in centimeters and when in meters
Building a mental sense of how long a centimeter and a meter are
howToPlay: Read the question, like 'About how long is a crayon?'
Picture how big the real thing is.
Tap the estimate that makes sense — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Estimate lengths in centimeters and meters — the focus of Common Core 2.MD.A.3
Match objects to a reasonable size and the right unit
Build the measurement intuition that makes later measuring meaningful

about: Working from tally marks or picture icons, children stack bars for forest finds — leaves, berries, acorns, pinecones, and mushrooms — across up to four categories, then read the graph to answer questions like how many more leaves than berries or how many in two categories together. It's a free, interactive Grade 2 data activity that runs in the browser, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is that a graph is a tool you build and then use. First the child turns counts into bars of the right height, even fixing a bar that is off; then they interpret the finished graph to compare, put together, and take apart amounts — and one round asks them to pick the graph that matches the data, proving they can read it back. Building before reading makes the bars meaningful instead of decorative.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.MD.D.10 — drawing a bar graph for up to four categories and solving simple put-together, take-apart, and compare problems using the information in the graph. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Turning tally marks or picture counts into bars of the right height
Building and fixing a bar graph for up to four categories
Reading the graph to find how many more or how many fewer
Putting two categories together to find a total from the graph
howToPlay: Read the tallies or icons and stack each bar one unit at a time.
Build the graph so every bar shows the right amount.
Read the finished graph to answer the question — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Draw a bar graph for up to four categories — the focus of Common Core 2.MD.D.10
Solve compare, put-together, and take-apart problems using a graph
Build the data sense that connects counting to reading charts and graphs

about: Gus the gopher is always restocking and selling at his busy snack cart — he sold 45 nuts and gave 8 away, picked 23 berries and 15 more, packed 27 apples with 36 cherries — and the child reads each story, works out the sum or difference within 100, and types the answer on the keypad. It's a free, interactive Grade 2 math activity that runs right in the browser, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is fluency with two-digit addition and subtraction, including problems that cross a ten — 27 + 36, 19 + 47, 45 − 8, and 60 − 25 all need regrouping, while 23 + 15 and 70 − 40 do not. Because the answer is typed rather than chosen from options, there is no guessing from a list: the child has to actually compute. Wrapping each problem in a real selling-and-restocking story keeps the arithmetic meaningful instead of abstract.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.NBT.B.5 — fluently adding and subtracting within 100 using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Adding two-digit numbers within 100, including sums that cross a ten
Subtracting two-digit numbers within 100, including problems that need regrouping
Pulling the numbers and the operation out of a short word problem
Typing an exact answer instead of picking from a list of choices
howToPlay: Read Gus's snack-cart story and look at the number sentence — is he adding or taking away?
Work out the answer within 100, then type it on the keypad and press Check.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Add and subtract two-digit numbers within 100 fluently — the focus of Common Core 2.NBT.B.5
Decide whether a story calls for adding or subtracting before computing
Build the place-value strategies that make regrouping feel natural

about: Marina the lighthouse-cat sends each little boat to its nearest round-number harbor: a boat sits at a spot on a number line — 63, 47, 24, or larger numbers like 247, 360, and 480 — and the child taps the harbor it is closest to, rounding to the nearest ten or hundred. It's a free, interactive Grade 3 math activity that plays in the browser, with no sign-up.

The heart of the activity is the halfway point. Some rounds ask the child to find the buoy in the middle between two harbors first — is 45 the halfway mark between 40 and 50? — so they can see which side the boat falls on. That focus is what makes rounding make sense rather than a rule to memorize, and it handles the tricky case where a number like 75 sits right on the line and rounds up. The child reads the position on the number line and decides; they do not just look at the last digit in isolation.
It is aligned to Common Core 3.NBT.A.1 — using place-value understanding to round whole numbers to the nearest 10 or 100. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Locating a number's position between two round-number harbors on a number line
Finding the halfway point between two tens or two hundreds
Rounding to the nearest ten and to the nearest hundred
Handling the round-up case when a number sits exactly halfway
howToPlay: Look at where the boat sits on the number line between the harbors.
Find the halfway buoy, decide which harbor the boat is closer to, and tap it.
A warm check confirms a correct choice and offers an easy retry when needed.
learningGoals: Round whole numbers to the nearest 10 and 100 using a number line — the focus of Common Core 3.NBT.A.1
Use the halfway point to decide which way a number rounds
Understand rounding as position on the line, not just a digit rule

about: Hattie the hedgehog runs the lost-and-found, where everything belongs to one owner — the dog's bone, the cat's ball, the bird's nest, the king's crown — and each round names an owner and the thing they own so the child can tap the word that shows ONE owner owns it. It's a free, interactive Grade 1 grammar activity that runs in the browser, with no account.

The big idea is the singular possessive: when one owner owns something, we add an apostrophe and an s. The child has to spot the form with the apostrophe in the right place rather than a plain plural that just adds s, so the choice turns on punctuation and meaning, not just spelling. Tying each one to a found object keeps the abstract apostrophe rule grounded in who the thing belongs to.
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.1.b — using singular possessive nouns, formed with an apostrophe and s. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Forming a singular possessive by adding an apostrophe and s
Telling a possessive (dog's) apart from a plain plural (dogs)
Matching an owner to the thing they own in a short phrase
Noticing where the apostrophe belongs in the word
howToPlay: Read who owns the thing — the dog and its bone, the king and the crown.
Tap the word that shows ONE owner owns it, then press Check.
A warm check confirms a correct choice and offers an easy retry when needed.
learningGoals: Use singular possessive nouns with an apostrophe and s — the focus of Common Core L.1.1.b
Recognize the difference between a possessive and a plural
Build the punctuation sense that early writing depends on

about: Hazel the heron builds a little word-bridge between two ideas: each round shows a sentence with a blank — 'I packed a hat ___ a coat,' 'I wore my boots ___ it was raining' — and the child taps the joining word that makes the two parts fit: and, but, because, or so. It's a free, interactive Grade 1 grammar activity that plays in the browser, with no sign-up.

The big idea is that different joining words signal different relationships. And simply adds one idea to another, but shows a contrast, because gives a reason, and so shows a result — so the child cannot pick by sound alone but has to read the whole sentence and feel how the two parts connect. The rounds move from simple adding and contrasting to cause-and-result, so the same skill stretches gradually.
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.1.g — using frequently occurring conjunctions to join words and ideas. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Choosing and, but, because, or so to fit a sentence
Telling a contrast (but) apart from a reason (because) or a result (so)
Reading both halves of a sentence before deciding how they connect
Joining two ideas into one sentence that makes sense
howToPlay: Read the sentence with the blank in the middle.
Tap the joining word — and, but, because, or so — that makes both parts fit, then press Check.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Use common conjunctions to join words and ideas — the focus of Common Core L.1.1.g
Match the joining word to the relationship between two ideas
Build the sentence-combining skill that fluent writing relies on

about: Hopper the frog adds and subtracts by hopping along a number line of lily pads — Hopper sits on 6 and hops forward 8, or sits on 80 and hops back 50 — and the child builds the move: place the start, point the hop forward to add or back to take away, choose the hop size, and find where Hopper lands. It's a free, interactive Grade 2 math activity that runs in the browser, with no account.

The big idea is representing a sum or difference as a jump on a number line, the model behind 2.MD.B.6. Because the child sets the direction and the size of the hop themselves, the number line stops being a picture to look at and becomes a tool they operate — and the decoy landing spots mean they have to track the actual jump, not guess a nearby number. The activity scales from hops of 2 and 3 up to hops of 10 across a line to 100.
It is aligned to Common Core 2.MD.B.6 — representing whole-number sums and differences within 100 on a number-line diagram. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Showing addition as a forward hop and subtraction as a hop back
Choosing the correct hop size and starting point on the number line
Finding the landing number after a jump within 100
Reading a number line as a tool for computing, not just a picture

Point the hop forward to add or back to take away, set the hop size, and find where he lands; then press Check.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Represent sums and differences within 100 on a number-line diagram — the focus of Common Core 2.MD.B.6
Connect adding to forward jumps and subtracting to backward jumps
Build the number-line model that supports later mental math

about: Inky the octopus makes books with ink — both the words and the pictures — so when Inky writes a story about a brave little tugboat, draws a sleepy dragon, or reads a bedtime story about the moon, the child taps whose job that is: author, illustrator, or reader. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten reading activity that plays in the browser, with no sign-up.

The big idea is the two roles that make a book, the focus of RL.K.6. By matching the action (writing, drawing, reading) to the person, the child learns that an author and an illustrator are different jobs, and that reading is something the child does. The 'reader' choice keeps the activity honest — the child has to think about the job, not just flip between two answers.
It is aligned to Common Core RL.K.6 — naming the author and illustrator of a story and defining the role of each in telling the story. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Knowing that the author writes the words of a book
Knowing that the illustrator draws the pictures
Matching an action — writing, drawing, reading — to the right person
Understanding the reader's own role in enjoying a book
howToPlay: Look at the job Inky is doing — writing words, drawing pictures, or reading.
Tap whose job it is: author, illustrator, or reader, then press Check.
A warm check confirms a correct choice and offers an easy retry when needed.
learningGoals: Name the author and illustrator and tell what each one does — the focus of Common Core RL.K.6
Tell apart the job of writing words from the job of drawing pictures
Build the book awareness that early read-aloud and reading depend on

about: Jasper the jay packs the just-right thing for each moment: a short real-life situation appears — it is raining, your feet are cold, you want to cut the paper — and the child taps the picture of what they would use, like an umbrella, a sock, or scissors. It's a free, interactive Grade 1 vocabulary activity that runs in the browser, with no account.

The big idea is connecting words to how things are really used in life, the focus of L.1.5.c. The wrong pictures are real objects too — a fan, a cup, a bed, an apple — so the child cannot win by picking 'the only sensible-looking thing'; they have to think about what the situation actually calls for. That match between a word and its real-world use is exactly the vocabulary depth this standard is after.
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.5.c — identifying real-life connections between words and their use. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Connecting a word to how the object is used in real life
Matching a need — staying dry, keeping feet warm, writing — to the right tool
Choosing the fitting object from several real, familiar choices
Building everyday vocabulary tied to common situations

Tap the picture of what you would use, then press Check.
A warm check confirms a correct choice and offers an easy retry when needed.
learningGoals: Identify real-life connections between words and their use — the focus of Common Core L.1.5.c
Match an everyday situation to the object it calls for
Deepen word knowledge beyond simple definitions

about: By lantern-light, Juniper the hedgehog tells a tiny fable — the Tortoise and the Hare, the Ant and the Grasshopper, the Lion and the Mouse, the Boy Who Cried Wolf — then asks the big question, and the child taps the card that states the lesson. It's a free, interactive Grade 1 reading activity that plays in the browser, with no sign-up.

The big idea is finding a story's central message, which means looking past the plot. The three cards are built to test exactly that: one states the moral, one is just a detail that happened in the story, and one is a wrong lesson that sounds plausible but the story does not teach. So a child cannot pick by repeating a line they remember — they have to decide what the whole story is really about.
It is aligned to Common Core RL.1.2 — retelling stories and demonstrating understanding of their central message or lesson. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Finding the lesson a story teaches, not just what happened in it
Telling the central message apart from a single story detail
Rejecting a lesson that sounds right but the story does not support
Listening to a short fable from beginning to end before deciding
howToPlay: Read or listen to Juniper's short fable all the way through.
Tap the card that tells the story's lesson — not a detail, not a wrong moral — then press Check.
A warm check confirms a correct choice and offers an easy retry when needed.
learningGoals: Identify the central message or lesson of a story — the focus of Common Core RL.1.2
Separate the main lesson from the events and details of the plot
Build the comprehension habit of asking what a story means

about: Inchie the inchworm measures garden objects by laying helper-worms end to end: along a pencil, a leaf, a ribbon, a crayon, or a carrot, the child places identical units with no gaps and no overlaps, then taps each helper to count how many long the object is. It's a free, interactive Grade 1 measurement activity that runs in the browser, with no account.

The big idea is that length is the number of same-size units that fit, the focus of 1.MD.A.2. The rounds make the rules visible by breaking them: one has a sneaky gap to scootch closed, one has helpers overlapping that need room, one offers a wrong-size decoy unit to reject, one starts off the tip, and one even measures the same leaf with big units and then little units to show that smaller units give a bigger count. The child does the laying and counting, so the measuring principles are discovered, not just told.
It is aligned to Common Core 1.MD.A.2 — measuring a length as the number of same-size length units laid end to end with no gaps or overlaps. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Laying same-size units end to end with no gaps and no overlaps
Starting the first unit right at the object's edge
Counting the units to give the length of an object
Seeing that smaller units make a larger count for the same object

Understand that gaps, overlaps, and mixed units give a wrong measurement
Build the unit-iteration idea behind reading rulers later

about: Linc the lizard links facts into a chain: a first fact appears — 'First, you plant a seed,' 'It rains on the dry grass,' 'You push the swing hard' — and the child taps the fact that connects to it, either what happens next or what it makes happen. learningGoals: Describe the connection between two facts or events — the focus of Common Core RI.K.3
Tell a sequence connection apart from a cause-and-effect one
Build early comprehension of how informational text holds together

about: Shelly the hermit crab measures shells and shows their lengths on a tide-line — a line plot scaled from 1 to 8 — and the child reads the X's stacked over each number to answer how many are 5 long, which length is most common, or how much longer the longest is than the shortest, and in other rounds places a new X. learningGoals: Read and build a measurement line plot in whole-number units — the focus of Common Core 2.MD.D.9
Compare lengths and find the most common length from the data
Connect each measurement to a single mark on the plot

about: Mama Duck calls the morning roll at Quack Creek, asking for an exact number of ducklings — send six, send eight, or none at all on a sleepy morning — and the child counts them out one by one from the raft, then signs the roll by tracing that number in the mud. It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.B.5 — counting to answer 'how many?' for objects in a line, an array, a scattered arrangement, or up to a given number. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.

Counting scattered objects and small groups that add to a total
Tracing the numeral that matches the count, including zero

A warm check confirms a correct count and offers an easy retry when needed.
learningGoals: Count to answer 'how many?' for up to ten objects — the focus of Common Core K.CC.B.5
Count an exact set even when objects are scattered or mixed
Connect counting a group to writing the matching numeral

about: Mango the monkey knows the special name for a group of animals — a herd of cows, a school of fish, a pack of wolves — so the child looks at the animal, then taps the word that names a whole group of them. The big idea is collective nouns, the focus of L.2.1.a. The three choices are all real group words — herd, flock, pack, swarm, school, pride, bunch — so the child cannot pick by ruling out nonsense; they have to know which group word belongs to which animal. Covering bees in a swarm, lions in a pride, and even grapes in a bunch shows that English has a rich, specific vocabulary for groups.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.1.a — using collective nouns. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Naming the group word for a familiar animal
Telling apart real group words like herd, flock, pack, and swarm
Matching the specific collective noun to the right animal
Building precise vocabulary for naming groups of things

Tap the word that names a whole group of them, then press Check.

learningGoals: Use collective nouns to name groups — the focus of Common Core L.2.1.a
Know which group word goes with which animal
Grow a richer, more exact vocabulary

about: Maple the mouse divides cookies two ways: in sharing rounds the child deals cookies equally onto a set number of plates — 12 cookies onto 3 plates — and in packing rounds the child packs them into boxes that each hold the same number, like 18 cookies into boxes of 6, and finds how many boxes are needed. It's a free, interactive Grade 3 math activity that runs in the browser, with no sign-up.

The big idea is the two meanings of division. Sharing asks 'how many in each group?' when you know the number of groups, while grouping asks 'how many groups?' when you know the size of each — and seeing both with the same kind of cookie problem shows that 12 ÷ 4 can answer either question. Because the child actually deals or packs the cookies, the division answer becomes a thing they can see and count, not a fact to recall.
It is aligned to Common Core 3.OA.A.2 — interpreting whole-number quotients as objects shared equally into groups or as the number of equal groups. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Sharing a number of objects equally to find how many in each group
Packing objects into equal groups to find how many groups there are
Seeing division as both 'how many in each' and 'how many groups'
Connecting the picture of equal groups to a division answer
howToPlay: Read whether Maple is sharing cookies onto plates or packing them into boxes.

learningGoals: Interpret a division answer as sharing or as grouping — the focus of Common Core 3.OA.A.2
Tell apart 'how many in each group' from 'how many groups'
Build the equal-groups meaning behind division and multiplication

about: At Marina the otter's news desk, a good headline says what a story is mostly about — the child reads a short three-sentence article, like how bees make honey or how a frog grows up, then taps the card that names its main topic. The big idea is finding the main topic, which means seeing the whole point rather than one part. The three cards are built to test it: one states the topic, one is a true detail pulled from the article, and one is off the page entirely — spiders spin webs, camels rarely drink. So the child cannot win by tapping the sentence that 'sounds like the story'; they have to decide what all of it is about, not just one fact it mentions.
It is aligned to Common Core RI.2.2 — identifying the main topic of a multi-paragraph text. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Reading a short informational passage for its overall point
Naming what the whole text is mostly about
Telling the main topic apart from a single supporting detail
Rejecting a choice that is off-topic, even if it sounds factual
howToPlay: Read Marina's short article all the way through.
Tap the card that names its main topic — not a small detail, not something off the page — then press Check.
A warm check confirms a correct choice and offers an easy retry when needed.
learningGoals: Identify the main topic of an informational text — the focus of Common Core RI.2.2
Separate the main topic from the details that support it
Build the comprehension habit of summarizing what a text is about

about: Playing story detective with Marlo the raccoon, children read a short three-sentence story, then a clue card states something about a character — "Mira is brave" or "Theo is careful" — and they tap the one detail that proves it, across cases covering brave, kind, curious, careful, patient, honest, generous, and hardworking. The whole point is finding evidence, not just any true sentence. When the card says Nina is generous, the proof is "She gave two stickers to her friend" — not the true-but-unrelated facts that the stickers were shaped like stars or that Nina kept one for herself. Each round offers one supporting detail and two real details from the same story that simply do not show the trait, so a child has to read closely and ask, "Which line actually proves this?"

practices: Connect a character trait word like brave, patient, or honest to the action that shows it

Read a short story closely and reread to find supporting evidence
Notice that what a character does tells you what they are like
howToPlay: Read Marlo's three-sentence story, then read the clue card that names a trait, such as "Sam is kind."
Tap the detail from the story that proves it — the action that shows the trait, not just a true detail like the color of someone's boots.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Describe a character using key details from the story — the focus of Common Core RL.1.3
Support a claim about a character with evidence rather than a guess
Build the close-reading habit of going back to the text for proof

about: Children see addition cards like 4 + 7 and 7 + 4, or 5 + 9 and 9 + 5, and link each addition to the same two numbers added the other way — tap one card, then tap its swapped twin, and the matched pair connects. The big idea is the commutative property: 4 + 7 and 7 + 4 both make 11, so the order of the addends does not change the total. Each round shows six cards — three swapped pairs jumbled together — so children work out the totals and notice which additions use the very same numbers flipped around. They are not matching identical cards; they are recognizing that two different-looking sums are equal.
It is aligned to Common Core 1.OA.B.3 — using properties of operations, like the commutative property, as strategies to add. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Recognize that addends can be added in any order for the same total

Match each addition to its swapped twin among jumbled cards
Use the turn-around fact as a strategy for adding more easily
howToPlay: Look at the six addition cards and work out which ones use the same two numbers in a different order.
Tap an addition like 3 + 6, then tap its swapped twin 6 + 3, and watch the pair link.

learningGoals: Apply the commutative property of addition — the focus of Common Core 1.OA.B.3
Understand that changing the order of the addends keeps the total the same
Use turn-around facts to make adding within 20 quicker and more confident

about: Children read a comparison like 247 ___ 274 or 583 ___ 419, then match it to the symbol that makes it true — less than (<) or greater than (>) — by tapping the comparison card and then the right symbol. The big idea is to compare by place value, hundreds first. Pairs are chosen so children cannot rely on a quick glance: numbers like 655 and 658 share the same hundreds and tens, so the ones digit decides, while 480 and 408 force a look at the tens. Use place value, hundreds first, to decide which number is greater
Build confident number sense with numbers up to 1000

about: Children solve cards like ? + 4 = 9, 8 + ? = 11, ? − 3 = 4, and 10 − ? = 6, then tap the equation and the number that completes it to link the pair. It's a free, interactive Grade 1 math activity that runs right in the browser, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is that the unknown can sit anywhere — a missing addend, a missing number to subtract, the starting number, or the total — so a child has to think the relationship through each time rather than always "adding to find the answer." about: Children link the cards that show the same value — the numeral (305), the number in words (three hundred five), and the expanded form (300 + 5) — tapping one card, then a card that matches its value, until the trio is connected. about: Children help Granny mend torn storybook pages by meaning, not just by sounds — filling a missing word so a sentence makes sense, fixing a word that breaks the sense, following who a pronoun means, placing a cat under or on a quilt, matching a sentence to the right picture, and putting three story strips in order — and each mended page warms from grey into color. about: Mim, a sleepy little cloud-friend, has spilled a basket of treasures, and children help sort each picture back where it belongs — a dog with the animals, an apple with the foods, a car with the vehicles, and later hats with clothing and a star with the shapes. about: Mochi the dumpling is hungry, and children feed it exactly the number of treats asked for — tapping the dish to drop one treat at a time into the bowl, 3 strawberries, 5 cookies, 4 cherries, on up to 10 muffins, then checking. It is aligned to Common Core L.2.4.c — using a known root word as a clue to the meaning of an unknown word in the same family. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Recognizing the smaller root word inside a bigger word
Choosing the word that grows from a given root, like player from play
Telling a true root-family word apart from look-alikes and sound-alikes
Using a familiar root as a clue to a new word's meaning
howToPlay: Read the root word at the start of the round.
Tap the bigger word that grows from it, watching out for words that only look or sound alike.
A warm check confirms a correct choice and offers an easy retry, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Use a known root word as a clue to a related word's meaning — the focus of Common Core L.2.4.c
Understand that words grow into families from a shared root
Build the word-analysis habit that vocabulary growth depends on

about: Wiggles the caterpillar hands over scrambled word tiles — 'big,' 'dog,' 'The,' 'runs.' — and a picture of the subject, and the child arranges them into "The big dog runs." It's a free, interactive Grade 1 grammar activity that runs in the browser with no account.

The whole idea is that a complete sentence has an order and a shape: it starts with a capital letter, has a naming word and an action word in the middle, and ends with a period. The capital is baked onto the starting tile and the period onto the last word, so the child focuses on putting the words in an order that makes sense — building real, complete sentences like "A little cat naps" and "Six brown hens peck" rather than just stacking words.
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.1.j — producing and expanding complete simple sentences (with L.K.1.b nouns and verbs). No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Putting scrambled words in an order that makes a complete sentence
Starting a sentence with a capital and ending it with a period
Including a naming word and an action word in each sentence
Reading the built sentence to check that it makes sense
howToPlay: Look at the picture and the scrambled word tiles.
Tap the tiles in order to build the sentence — capital first, period last — then press Check.
Not quite? Rearrange and try again as many times as you like, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Produce a complete simple sentence in the right word order — the focus of Common Core L.1.1.j
Understand that a sentence needs a naming word, an action word, a capital, and an end mark
Build the sentence-writing foundation for early composing

about: Gentle Dr. Plume's patients are muddled sentences, each with one ailment — a missing capital in "my dog is happy," no end mark after "The sun is hot," or "She run to school" — and the child finds the trouble and makes the repair. It's a free, interactive Grade 2 grammar activity that runs in the browser with no account.

Each round practices a different convention, so children meet the real range of fixes: capitalizing the first word, adding the right end mark (a period, not a comma or question mark), correcting subject-verb agreement (run to runs), adding a missing verb ("The cat ___ milk" to drinks), reordering jumbled words into "The dog runs fast," removing an extra word in "My mom she cooks," and splitting a run-on into two sentences. The wrong options are real near-misses, so the child has to diagnose what is actually wrong.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.1 — demonstrating command of standard English grammar and usage. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Capitalizing the first word and ending a telling sentence with a period
Fixing subject-verb agreement, like 'She runs' instead of 'She run'
Adding a missing verb and removing an extra or repeated word
Reordering jumbled words and splitting a run-on into two sentences
howToPlay: Read the muddled sentence and find what is wrong.
Make the repair — capitalize, add a mark or word, fix the verb, reorder, delete, or split.
A warm check confirms a correct fix and offers an easy retry, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Apply the conventions of standard English grammar and usage — the focus of Common Core L.2.1
Recognize and repair common sentence problems in writing
Build the editing habit that clear writing depends on

about: Tilly the shop cat keeps her ribbons on far-apart shelves where you can't lay them side by side, so the child reads each one — red, blue, green, yellow — against a measuring cord and taps the longest, the shortest, or the one just as long as the cord. It's a free, interactive Grade 1 measurement activity that runs in the browser with no account.

The big idea is comparing length indirectly: when two things are too far apart to line up, a third object — the cord — lets you compare them anyway. Across the rounds the question changes between longest, shortest, and just-as-long-as-the-cord, so a child has to read each ribbon's length against the cord rather than guessing by a quick glance, which is exactly the reasoning that ordering objects by length builds.
It is aligned to Common Core 1.MD.A.1 — ordering objects by length and comparing two objects indirectly using a third. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Comparing the length of objects that cannot be placed side by side
Using a measuring cord as a third object to compare two others
Choosing the longest, the shortest, or the one equal to the cord
Ordering several ribbons by how long they are
howToPlay: Read each colored ribbon against Tilly's measuring cord.
Tap the longest, the shortest, or the ribbon that is just as long as the cord, depending on the question.
A warm check confirms a correct choice and offers an easy retry, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Order objects by length and compare two indirectly using a third — the focus of Common Core 1.MD.A.1
Understand that a measuring tool lets you compare things you cannot line up
Build the length-reasoning foundation that later measurement work depends on

about: Pesto the parrot needs the word of exactly the right strength at his soup stall — warm, toasty, hot, scalding all mean heat, but the shade matters — so the child reads what a customer needs ("only just cool enough to sip") and taps the right-strength word. It's a free, interactive Grade 1 vocabulary activity that runs in the browser with no account.

The big idea is distinguishing near-synonyms by degree, and the activity stretches it several ways: choosing the word that fits a sentence (a quiet voice versus a booming one, a damp towel versus a soaked one), ordering a set like warm-toasty-hot-scalding from weakest to strongest, finding the word that falls between two others, and choosing the right way to look — peek, glance, stare, or glare — for how someone feels. Because the words are so close in meaning, a child has to weigh strength, not just pick any word that fits the topic.
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.5.d — distinguishing shades of meaning among verbs and adjectives that differ by degree (also L.2.5.b). No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Choosing the word of the right strength to fit a sentence
Ordering near-synonyms from weakest to strongest, like warm to scalding
Finding the word that falls between two others in strength
Picking the right way to look — peek, glance, stare, or glare — for a feeling
howToPlay: Read what the customer needs, or the set of similar words.
Tap the right-strength word, order the ladder, find the in-between word, or choose the right way to look.
A warm check confirms a correct choice and offers an easy retry, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Distinguish shades of meaning among related words that differ by degree — the focus of Common Core L.1.5.d
Understand that near-synonyms carry different amounts of strength
Build the precise word-choice sense that stronger speaking and writing depend on

about: Mim the glow-smith forges light by fusing small glowing pattern blocks — triangles and rhombi — to fill a blank lantern outline, making a rhombus, a trapezoid, a hexagon, and more. It's a free, interactive Grade 1 geometry activity that runs in the browser with no account.

The big idea is composing shapes — that bigger shapes are built from smaller ones, and the same shape can be built more than one way. The rounds go beyond simply filling an outline: children re-forge the same hexagon a new way, re-compose a shape into a long bar, cover a space using only triangles, and grow a partly-built shape into a finished hexagon. Because a triangle and a rhombus can both help fill a space, a child has to choose and arrange pieces that actually fit, not just drop blocks in.
It is aligned to Common Core 1.G.A.2 — composing two-dimensional shapes to create a composite shape (also K.G.B.6). No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Building a larger shape from triangle and rhombus pattern blocks
Filling a target outline with pieces that fit, with no gaps or overlaps
Making the same shape more than one way, and re-forging it into a new shape
Covering a space using a chosen kind of block, or finishing a partly-built shape
howToPlay: Look at the blank lantern outline you need to forge.
Fuse triangles and rhombi to fill it — or re-forge the same shape a new way.
Not quite? Rearrange the pieces and try again, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Compose two-dimensional shapes into a larger composite shape — the focus of Common Core 1.G.A.2
Understand that bigger shapes are made of smaller ones, often in more than one way
Build the spatial-reasoning foundation for later geometry and fraction work

about: Pim and Bo scoop moon-beads into their jars at The Sharing Jar, and one jar always ends up fuller — so the child finds the missing number that makes it fair: how many more the quiet jar needs, how big the gap is, or how many there were to start, tapped on tiles from 0 to 10. It's a free Grade 1 math activity that runs in the browser with no account.

The numbers stay small, but the unknown moves around — sometimes it is the amount to add, sometimes the difference, sometimes the starting amount that has to be uncovered. That is the whole point: the child is not just adding two numbers, but figuring out which part is missing and how to find it, using counting-on and fact-family thinking. Saying the number out loud before tapping it ties the spoken answer to the written numeral.
It is aligned to Common Core 1.OA.D.8 — finding the unknown number in an addition or subtraction situation, in any position. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Find the missing number when the unknown is the part to add, the difference, or the start
Use counting-on and fact families to make two amounts equal
Work out how much more one group has than another within 10 and a little beyond
Connect a spoken number to the written numeral by saying it before tapping
howToPlay: Read the two jars and the question — how many more beads does the quiet friend need to be fair?
Work it out, say the kind number, then tap that numeral on the tiles from 0 to 10 and press Check.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Find the unknown number in an addition or subtraction story — the focus of Common Core 1.OA.D.8.
Understand that the missing part can sit anywhere — the sum, an addend, or the starting amount.
Build the equal-and-fair number sense that early addition and subtraction depend on.

about: Hopper hops across a row of numbered lily pads with one pad left empty, and the child reads the jumps between them — +5, +10, or +100, forward or backward — to find the number on the blank pad. It's a free, interactive Grade 2 math activity that runs in the browser with no account.

Skip-counting is more than reciting fives and tens — it is noticing the steady rhythm of a pattern and using it to predict. Because the empty pad is sometimes in the middle and sometimes at the end, and because one round starts on an off-multiple like 3, the child cannot rely on a memorized chant; they have to read the actual pads and add or subtract the step. That is the bridge from counting to place value and later to multiplication.
It is aligned to Common Core 2.NBT.A.2 — counting within 1000 and skip-counting by 5s, 10s, and 100s. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Count forward and backward by 5s, 10s, and 100s along a number sequence
Find a missing number in the middle or at the end of a skip-counting pattern
Notice the step size between numbers and name which jump is being made
Skip-count starting from off-multiple numbers, not just from zero
howToPlay: Read the numbered lily pads and find the empty one.
Work out the +5, +10, or +100 jump (or the backward hop), then tap the number that goes on the blank pad.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s within 1000 — the focus of Common Core 2.NBT.A.2.
Use the step in a pattern to predict the number that comes next or fills a gap.
Build the counting fluency that later place-value and multiplication work rely on.

about: Starting at a marked dot, the child traces each letter stroke by stroke — c, s, i, t, a, d, and a big capital S — first with the path shown to guide the hand, then again with it hidden. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten handwriting warm-up that plays in the browser as a friendly complement to paper practice.

Good handwriting starts with consistent stroke order, not just the right shape, so the activity always cues where to begin and which part comes first — the round part of a before its stick, the tall stick of b before its bump. The two-step design (guided, then unguided) is what builds independence: the child first feels the motion, then reproduces it from memory. This is motor practice, not a quiz.
It is aligned to Common Core L.K.1.a — printing many upper- and lowercase letters. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Form lowercase letters like c, s, a, d, b, and f with correct stroke order
Start each letter at the right point and take its strokes in sequence
Move from a guided trace to forming the letter with the path hidden
Connect each letter to a word that begins with it, like c for cat
howToPlay: Start on the dot and trace the letter stroke by stroke while the path is shown.
Then trace the same letter again with the path hidden, forming it on your own.
Take your time — there is no timer and no score, just steady practice.
learningGoals: Print upper- and lowercase letters with correct formation — the focus of Common Core L.K.1.a.
Understand that letters are built from strokes taken in a set order.
Build the fine-motor control and letter memory that handwriting depends on.

about: The child is Sock's voice, telling Shadow — a puppet behind the curtain who can't see the tray — exactly which object to fetch, adding a color, size, or position word when there are two cups or two hats to tell apart. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten speaking game that runs in the browser with no sign-up, meant to be played aloud with a grown-up.

The trap runs both ways, and that is the lesson: say too little and Shadow holds up the wrong object or two at once; pile on too many words and Shadow forgets half the message. The child chooses meaning-chips — color, size, position, the object name — to build the smallest clear description, then taps Tell Shadow and watches whether the puppet fetches correctly. One round even asks the child to name a feeling and its reason. Because this is speaking practice, the spoken part is meant to be done aloud with a grown-up.
It is aligned to Common Core SL.K.6 — speaking audibly and expressing thoughts, feelings, and ideas clearly. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Add the color, size, or position word that singles out one object from look-alikes
Say just enough to be clear — not too vague and not too many words
Notice when a listener who cannot see needs more information
Name a feeling and the reason for it in a clear, complete message
howToPlay: Look at the tray and decide which object Shadow should fetch and what makes it different.
Tap the meaning-chips to build a clear description, then tap Tell Shadow and check whether the right object is fetched.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Express an idea clearly so a listener understands — the focus of Common Core SL.K.6.
Understand that a good message has enough detail to be clear, but no extra clutter.
Build the describing-and-explaining habits that clear speaking depends on.

about: Is it still a triangle if it's red, big, or tilted? One shape is named each round, and the child drags every shape into the right box by deciding what it IS, not how it looks — sorting real triangles from squares, pentagons, and hexagons. It's a free, interactive Grade 1 geometry activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The whole idea is the difference between a defining attribute and a non-defining one. A triangle is defined by having three sides — full stop — while being red, big, or tilted is just how this particular triangle happens to look. By sorting examples against tempting non-examples, the child learns to ignore the surface and judge by the property that actually matters. That is the start of real geometric reasoning.

It is aligned to Common Core 1.G.A.1 — distinguishing defining attributes from non-defining attributes and building and drawing shapes that have them. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Decide whether a shape belongs to a named group by its number of sides
Tell a defining attribute (number of sides) from a non-defining one (color, size, direction)
Recognize triangles and quadrilaterals in many forms, not just the textbook example
Ignore look-alikes and judge a shape by what makes it that shape
howToPlay: Read the named shape — for example, triangle — at the top of the round.
Drag each shape into the right box by deciding whether it IS that shape, no matter its color, size, or direction.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Distinguish defining from non-defining attributes of shapes — the focus of Common Core 1.G.A.1.
Understand that a triangle stays a triangle when its color, size, or orientation changes.
Build the attribute-based reasoning that classifying and naming shapes depends on.

about: Each round drops a jumble of shapes — right and obtuse triangles, squares, rhombuses, irregular pentagons and hexagons — and the child counts the sides of each and drags it into the matching bin. It's a free, interactive Grade 2 geometry activity that plays in the browser with no sign-up.

The key move is counting the sides rather than matching a remembered picture, because a stretched or tilted five-sided shape is still a pentagon. By facing irregular and rotated shapes alongside the tidy ones, the child practices using the number of sides as the rule that names a polygon. That builds the vocabulary — quadrilateral, pentagon, hexagon — and the habit of analyzing shapes by their parts.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.G.A.1 — recognizing and drawing shapes with specified attributes such as a given number of sides, and identifying triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, and hexagons. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Count the sides of a shape to decide which polygon group it belongs to
Tell triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, and hexagons apart by their number of sides
Recognize the same polygon when it is irregular, stretched, or rotated
Use the words quadrilateral, pentagon, and hexagon correctly
howToPlay: Look at each shape and count how many sides it has.
Drag it into the matching bin — triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, or hexagons.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, and hexagons by their sides — the focus of Common Core 2.G.A.1.
Understand that the number of sides, not the look, names a polygon.
Build the shape vocabulary and side-counting habit that later geometry depends on.

about: Coco the koala shows a three-sound word like cat or dog broken into little boxes, with one box lit to mark the first, middle, or last sound, and the child hears the word and taps another picture that shares that same sound in that same spot. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten listening game that runs in the browser with no account.

This is phonemic awareness, the ear-only skill that comes before spelling: the child is not reading letters but pulling apart the beginning, middle-vowel, and ending sounds of a spoken word. Because one round asks for the first sound, another the middle, and another the last, the child learns that a word is a string of distinct sounds — that cat and cap share a beginning, while cat and bat share a middle and an end. The picture choices keep the focus on listening, not letters.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.K.2.d — isolating and pronouncing the initial, medial vowel, and final sounds in three-phoneme words. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Isolate the first, middle, or last sound in a short three-sound word
Match two pictures that share a sound in the same position
Hear that a word is made of separate sounds, not one block
Tell apart words that share a beginning from words that share an ending
howToPlay: Listen to Coco's word and notice which sound box is lit — first, middle, or last.
Tap the other picture whose name has the same sound in that same spot, then press Check.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Isolate the beginning, middle, and ending sounds of CVC words — the focus of Common Core RF.K.2.d.
Understand that a spoken word is built from separate sounds in order.
Build the sound-awareness foundation that decoding and spelling depend on.

about: Span the inchworm shows two labeled bars with their lengths in centimeters — a ribbon 8 cm beside a string 5 cm — and the child works out how much LONGER the longer one is, then types the difference on the keypad. It's a free, interactive Grade 2 measurement activity that runs in the browser with no account.

The skill is finding the difference between two measurements, which is subtraction wearing a measurement hat. The child reads both lengths, decides which is longer, and figures the gap (8 and 5 means 3 centimeters longer). Keeping the lengths visible as bars helps the child see the extra piece they are measuring, so the answer is grounded in a picture and not just a number sentence.
It is aligned to Common Core 2.MD.A.4 — measuring to determine how much longer one object is than another, expressed in a standard length unit. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Read two lengths given in centimeters and decide which is longer
Find how much longer one object is than another by taking the difference
Use subtraction to compare two measurements within 100
Type a measured answer in the correct unit
howToPlay: Read how long each bar is in centimeters.
Work out how much longer the longer one is, then type that difference on the keypad and press Check.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Find how much longer one object is than another — the focus of Common Core 2.MD.A.4.
Understand that comparing two lengths means finding the difference between them.
Build the measure-and-compare skill that later length and data work depend on.

about: A stuck firefly can only fly to stars the child has already counted, so starting from one lit star — not always at one — the child taps Count on to light each next numeral (eight… nine… ten…) and Wake it to settle her down, until a hidden constellation animal appears. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten counting game that runs in the browser with no account.

The big idea is counting on from a given number instead of restarting at one every time — a real leap for young counters. Because the starting star can be 6, 7, 11, or 12, the child has to know what comes next from there, not recite the whole sequence from the beginning. Saying each number as it lights links the spoken count to the written numeral and to the one-by-one motion of counting.
It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.A.2 — counting forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Count forward from a given number instead of starting at one
Say each number in order as the next star lights up
Fill the missing numbers between two known anchor numbers
Count a small set first, then keep counting on from that amount
howToPlay: Start at the one lit star and read the number it shows.
Tap Count on to fly the firefly forward one dark star at a time, then tap Wake it to land her — until the last star lights.
Take your time — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Count forward from a given number within the sequence — the focus of Common Core K.CC.A.2.
Understand that counting can begin anywhere, not only at one.
Build the counting-on fluency that addition and later number work depend on.

about: Dot the dragon shares a short three-picture story — The Lost Mitten, The Snatched Carrot, The Rainy Picnic — and the child taps which part is the START, the TROUBLE, and the FIX. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten reading activity that runs in the browser with no account.

The skill is recognizing the shape every story shares — a setting, a problem, and a solution — by matching each picture to its job in the tale. Because the child names the role rather than just retelling events, they begin to see story structure as a pattern they can use again and again. The same three roles appear across all three stories, so the idea transfers and is not tied to one plot.
It is aligned to Common Core RL.K.3 — identifying characters, settings, and major events in a story. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Identify the setting, the problem, and the solution in a short story
Match each picture to its job in the tale — start, trouble, or fix
Recognize the same story shape across different stories
Retell the major events of a story in order
howToPlay: Read or listen to Dot's three-picture story.
Tap which part is the START, the TROUBLE, or the FIX the question asks for, then press Check.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Identify the setting, problem, and solution and the major events of a story — the focus of Common Core RL.K.3.
Understand that stories follow a shape: a beginning, a problem, and a way it gets better.
Build the story-structure sense that comprehension and retelling depend on.

about: Stretch the giraffe loves the long, stretched-out vowels that say their own name — the a in cake, the e in bee, the i in pie — so the child taps a picture to hear its name, then taps the word with the long (or short) vowel the round asks for. Headphones are recommended for this free, interactive Grade 1 listening game, which runs in the browser with no account.

Because the answer lives in the sound, not the spelling, the child has to listen carefully and judge with their ears — does this vowel say its name, or make its short, clipped sound? Tapping to hear each word as many times as needed keeps the focus on the vowel itself. Telling long from short vowels is a foundation for sounding out and spelling words with confidence.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.1.2.a — distinguishing long from short vowel sounds in spoken single-syllable words. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Tell a long vowel that says its name from a short, clipped vowel
Listen to a spoken word and judge its vowel sound by ear
Identify the long or short vowel among picture-word choices
Hear the vowel as the heart of a single-syllable word
howToPlay: Tap a picture to hear its name — listen to the vowel in the middle.
Tap the word with the long (or short) vowel sound the question asks for, then press Check.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Distinguish long from short vowel sounds in spoken words — the focus of Common Core RF.1.2.a.
Understand that long vowels say their name while short vowels make a clipped sound.
Build the vowel-listening skill that sounding out and spelling depend on.

about: The child is the waiter when a customer speaks a compound order aloud — like two pancakes and a milk — first gathering it onto the tray, then saying it back as one full sentence by tapping each part and dropping in the golden "and" that joins them. It's a free, interactive Kindergarten speaking game that runs in the browser with no sign-up, meant to be played aloud with a grown-up.

The big idea is producing and expanding a complete sentence, with "and" as the coupler that links two parts into one. The child cannot win by naming a single food; they have to hold the whole order in mind, keep the right quantities, and join the pieces so the read-back is a full, correct sentence. Because this is oral language practice, the spoken read-back is meant to be done aloud with a grown-up.
It is aligned to Common Core L.K.1.f — producing and expanding complete sentences in shared language activities. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Listen to a whole order and gather all of its parts
Say a complete sentence that names each item and its quantity
Use "and" to join two parts into one compound sentence
Fix a wrong item or add a part to expand the sentence
howToPlay: Listen to the customer's order and tap the food pictures to gather the whole order on the tray.
Then say it back: tap each part into place and drop in the "and" so it makes one complete sentence, then press Check.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Produce and expand a complete compound sentence — the focus of Common Core L.K.1.f.
Understand that "and" joins two parts of a sentence into one.
Build the sentence-building and listening skills that clear speaking depends on.

about: Keep the base word steady and swap only its ending: the child hears a word, then taps -s, -ing, or -ed to build the new one — cat to cats, jump to jumping, play to played — with the wrong endings sitting right beside the right one. It's a free, interactive Grade 1 reading activity that runs in the browser with no account.

The skill is reading words with inflectional endings — recognizing the familiar base inside a longer word and the small ending that changes its job. By keeping the base word steady and swapping only the ending, the child sees that -s, -ed, and -ing each carry a meaning, and learns to read the whole word instead of stalling at the longer form. Hearing the finished word ties the spelling to its sound.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.1.3.f — reading words with inflectional endings. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Add -s, -ed, or -ing to a base word to build the right new word
Recognize the base word inside a longer word with an ending
Match the ending to its meaning — more than one, happening now, or already happened
Read the whole word, ending and all, instead of stopping at the base
howToPlay: Read the base word and tap Hear it to listen.
Tap the right ending — -s, -ed, or -ing — to build the word, then press Check.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Read words with the endings -s, -ed, and -ing — the focus of Common Core RF.1.3.f.
Understand that an ending changes a word's meaning while the base stays the same.
Build the word-analysis skill that fluent reading of longer words depends on.

about: Two vowels work together for one long sound, and the child spells the picture's word by tapping its sound chunks in order — b-oa-t, l-ea-f, j-ee-p, r-ai-n — choosing the vowel team as a single piece. It's a free, interactive Grade 1 reading activity that runs in the browser with no account.

The key idea is that a vowel team is one spelling unit for one long sound — two letters, but a single chunk the eye learns to grab. By building the word piece by piece and picking the team that matches the long vowel they hear, the child stops trying to sound out each letter separately and starts reading the pattern. That is a major step in decoding common long-vowel words.
